title: Rethinking Systemic Risk: An Orthogonal Interaction Framework Linking System‐Wide Disruption and Systemic Vulnerability
content:
Abstract

This paper proposes an integrative conceptual framework for understanding systemic risk as emerging in highly interconnected socio-ecological-technical systems. Previous research has often examined hazard-driven risk and vulnerability as separate analytical problems. We argue that systemic risk develops through their interaction within systems characterized by interdependence, nonlinearity, and feedback processes, properties that fundamentally differentiate systemic risk from traditional risk paradigms. We translate this integration into an orthogonal interaction model structured around three independent dimensions: mechanism, topology, and timing. The framework maps 27 interaction types onto three systemic-risk tiers according to their cascade potential, providing a diagnostic structure for distinguishing cascade-generating, pre-critical, and weak or buffering configurations. The framework synthesizes two complementary analytical perspectives that remain largely disconnected in the literature. The first approaches systemic risk as system-wide disruption resulting from cascading, compounding, and cross-system interactions. The second approach frames it through systemic vulnerability, that is, a persistent vulnerability core shaped by long-term socio-economic, institutional, cultural, and governance processes. Bringing these perspectives together shows how systemic risk emerges when disturbances activate pre-existing vulnerabilities through cascade-permissive interaction structures. This explains why moderate-magnitude hazards can trigger disproportionate impacts and why such events exhibit heavy-tailed loss distributions driven by interaction-induced feedback processes. We illustrate the analytical utility of the proposed framework through recent cascading disasters with major implications for risk governance. The framework shifts attention from hazard magnitude alone toward systemic vulnerability, interdependencies, and cascade-prone architectures, with direct implications for risk assessment and adaptation policy.
